[b]My playtime:[/b] I played this offline, but i think it took somewhere around 12-24h to finish the game.
[b]Grindy Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement:[/b] Yes (8 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Developer Response:[/b] No (last response is in 26 Feb, 2019).

[h1]Intro[/h1]
Hacknet is a hacking simulator game where you have to hack some ip address with the tools you had. Most of the hacking will be done through terminal although the game has some GUI that you can interact with.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Even though i said that you'll type your commands through terminal, it doesn't mean that you'll only have to look at it. There are some UI in the game that you can see, such as when you launch your tools or check the compromised system. I even think that the UI helped very well because i'm sure i don't want to browse all of the system directory from the command line; it took too much effort to type and check them all. You can also see the server location and connect to them without typing at all in case you forgot the ip or just too lazy to type the whole thing.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game's story is mostly told through an exchange of emails and reading files in a server. You'll investigate someone who has been lost for a long time, Bit, while uncovering a hidden secret that causes his disappearance. The story might look decent, but i'm quite impressed with the visuals at the end of the story.

The game also has additional files in the servers that you hacked in. I like to read some of them (especially the short ones) since they are pretty funny.

[h1]The game[/h1]
As a hacking simulator game, the game simulates the terminal very well. The basic is pretty much the same (ls, cd, cat, etc) while there are some custom commands mixed in. The game also has an auto complete feature although it's quite limited; you can't do auto complete for stuffs in other directory. Well, sometimes it works, but sometimes it don't. The game also doesn't support complicated command with arguments like rm -rf (remove everything in a directory) even though the game has missions like this. The limitations are pretty acceptable to me though.

Anyway, if you have no idea with anything that i said above, the game will help you to learn some terminal commands. If you're in windows, it's the thing that popped up when you press windows+r and then type cmd, except that the commands are for Linux OS and the like. Like how most terminals are, there is a help command that you can use to recognize all of the available commands and if you didn't notice it like i did, the help command actually has paging in it; you can type help 1, help 2, and help 3 to check most of the commands in the game. Most, because the help command won't tell you anything about what does your .exe file do.

Beside the basic commands, you'll also have .exe files. These files are usually what is installed in your computer and can be basically anything, from a browser to your game. However, most .exe files in this game is actually a tool that is used for hacking. You'll know how the things work if you read the instructions, which is obviously stored somewhere else. You'll usually get these .exe files by going through some servers and copying the files to your machine.

In this game, you'll need to read a lot. By a lot, i mean a lot. Really. You might need to understand some complicated stuffs or just know the general knowledge and the game will punish you severely if you don't know what are you doing. I mistook proxy servers and port for a while and i thought that i need 4 proxy servers to hack in a server although it actually asked me to open 4 ports. I got confused for a while before i noticed my mistake.

Sometimes, the game won't tell you what to do and you had to understand everything by yourself. One example is when a hacker suddenly attacked me. I didn't know what to do at that point because the tutorial (yes, there is a tutorial) only tells me how to hack.

As i said before, you'll usually hack a server. You'll have a lead in a form of ip address that you need to hack in and you'll check what you need to do to hack it. The game will usually tell you whether you have to connect to a proxy, guess a firewall, run one of your hacking tools to open a number of port required to get in, or all of them. Sometimes, the server owner will notice your break in and a timer will show up. You must finish your hacking, remove your traces, and logout before it reaches zero or you'll get a blue screen. The strange thing is, the game is a bit "buggy" on this. If you leave the server while running your hacking tools, the hacking will still be ongoing and you can do your second attempt with a head start. The stranger thing is, if the timer reach zero by the time you finish the hacking (and you haven't logged out yet), the hacking will also be finished after you deal with the blue screen and return to the server. Well, there are actually some more, but these two are the only thing that i had in my mind for now.

Since you'll use a lot of hacking tools, you might run out of memories. Some hacking tools take more memories than the others so you can't use them all at the same time. This helps to make the game more difficult although there is one place where you have to "cheat" your way through because you will never have the time to get in in the first place [spoiler](the CCC Hacksquad Filedump)[/spoiler].

The game's story has a two branching paths that will converge in the end. The other path requires you to really know what you're doing though; i won't be able to make it in if i didn't read a guide beforehand. The game also has some commands that are not available in help commands that might be useful in these cases. These additional commands are told after you beat the game and is supposed to be an additional command in case there is a new update in.

You'll mostly play the game by accepting quests and finishing them. There is also a few points in the game where you can choose the missions that you want to do. Sadly, there is a place where you can't choose them all and it kinda saddens me since it left the place with unfinished tasks.

Since you'll be hacking a lot of servers, there are some optional places that you can go to and some places might have some secrets in it. I had fun locating a lot of new servers that are not introduced in the main story although i'm not sure if i got all of them; sometimes, the secret is so well hidden that you have to read really carefully.

Pros:
- Uses mostly real terminal commands
- 2 branching paths
- Lots of secrets to explore

Cons:
- Leaving the server during a trace is kinda buggy
- You need to read a lot

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]
This is a nice hacking simulation game to spend your time with.

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to play hacking simulation game, buy this. You might have to know a little bit about terminals though; you can actually play it without knowing it at all but it might give you a harder time, especially if you don't like to learn and read.[/i]

review_text_raw:
So yeah. This game left me absolutely speechless. At 2AM. Ending sent shivers down my spine. And there's waaay more. Whilst decrypting one of the files i decided to check out its header. There was an IP of a server. It was NOT related to the mission. I wasn't even suposed to check the header. I wasn't curious or patient enough to follow this lead but it was there. The author of the game sates that every person we meet in the game CAN BE TRACKED DOWN!!! I trust him. 

Hacknet is a simulator situated really close to real hacking - true, but it's also something way bigger. It's an epic story. A possibility for a player to enforce the type of gameplay he desires. Yes - you can cooperate with a hacking group but in the meantime you can hack their server and read their personal e-mails. 

Don't get me wrong - this game is linear. You can't get to other endings. You can't make other people react to your actions. Even when you intentionally send a guy p.e: wrong password - he won't respond. Only "Mission incompleted" window will pop up. It's not even like the player thinks he can make the world respond - you don't have any illusion of sandbox. 

Still tough. The Game left me thinking. Not about the story of Bit. Not about the story of V. Not even about the genius of the maker, nooo... I was thinking: "What the hell am I going to do with my life now?". I am amazed. I am mesmerized. I approve. Brown, out!

review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.


[h1] RATING: 8.5/10 [/h1]

review_text_raw:
Full disclosure: I am a giant nerd. Grew up more on computers (and dogs!) than, like, ya know.... PEOPLE... The point is, if you put a terminal or a shell in front of me I get super excited and it's instantly, like, +5,000 to appreciation for thing.

ANYWAY.

This game is sublime. I think, oftentimes, if you look up hacking sims, you get to get stuff like Uplink, which is very good, certainly, and I DO recommend it, but Hacknet was made as a spiritual successor to it (by the dev's own confirmation), and I consider it better in every way. Uplink is a little more sandbox-y (think, like, a game that is entirely a radiant quest from Skyrim. Except, like... good. And dynamic); Hacknet actually has a story. There are a number of missions to do, and it's not linear in the sense that you have to do everything in order, but there are a couple factions you can go with and you'll get different tasks from them. It all culminates in the same storyline at the end, but I don't mean that as a negative. The writing is really good, the gameplay is engaging, and there are tons of little incidentals you can find for worldbuilding and extraneous fun (IRC logs are a really good example of this, and many of those are extremely well-observed; tech-heads, I can guarantee, will find some gems in there).

Essentially, you encounter external systems and learn to crack them. For various reasons. Everything from "delete this sensitive file" to "modify a file's contents" to "find out where this signal came from" to "cripple this server" and others. And that's just for starters. Eventually you start dealing with conspiracies, and your missions get really involved, having to crack multiple terminals, finding links between them, worming your way into other systems, finding user credentials, reading e-mails, finding synched external devices, etc, etc. You have to break through security before you can CRACK the system, naturally, and different systems have different layers requiring different programs to surpass. It's almost entirely SKiddying, for those of you who are also dorks like myself, but it's very entertainingly-done and the graphics built to illustrate Computer Happenings (R)(C) are really rad. I wouldn't be surprised if you needed a guide at some point, your first time through, but, well, put it this way: collaboration between agents is pretty common, so don't feel bad.

The interface is really cool, you CAN do just about everything with the mouse, if you're wired that way, but you can also use the console, which is my preferred way of doing things. There are multiple .sys overlays you can enable, as well, to change your GUI and layout, which adds a little customization (some of them done by commissioned artist). The expansion that's since come out is a lot of fun, and adds probably another four to six hours to a game that I'd say is around ten hours your first time through, if you know what you're doing. Decently replayable, too.

Finally, I will say that this is one of my favorite soundtracks I've ever heard. I've never seen a game before this that uses Vaporwave as its backing, but it makes a lot of sense; that's a really good genre for focus-demanding work, like this game presents. Also, they used HOME on the soundtrack, and they are one of my absolute favorites (shill, shill). I will also say, while the OST is extremely chill, they DO use one of the higher-octane tracks from Hotline Miami 2, and I daresay it fits even better here.

review_text_raw:
To be fair Uplink is better. This game is good because you get to use the keyboard. Uplink is a hacking game where keyboard is not used, so the biggest flaw is now solved. Problem is the game lacks a bit of adrenaline. 

1) Most servers don't trace you, so you can just hang around forever.
2) Its not clear where you are connected too. Once you hack a place is there opened forever. You don't even have to disconnect.
3) You clear your logs but not the disconnected log, which makes no sense. In Uplink you have to clear logs at origin and destination, seems more realistic.
4) Its too easy to go up the ranking. 
5) In Uplink you had money to worry about. Upgrade hardware and buy software. In Hacknet all you get is reputation, that also have no impact besides gettings invitations.
6) The game does not allow you to accept more than 1 mission.
7) The storyline is a bit broken. I made 1 mission that lead to a hacker invading my computer, that leads to another mission and to another mission and basically you cannot accept other mission while the "story" is leading you in 1 way. That made me join an organization and now I cannot finish the old missions. Basically I lost 3 missions, cannot be played.
8) The game UI is a bit limited. I cannot open a file and an email at the same time. Which makes very annoying to take note to things. Althought I cannot complain much on that, as in Uplink I really had a pen and paper next to me all the time, in this game I never used real paper so far.
9) Uplink allow you to do other stuff, such as Stock Market, browse any server, etc. Hacknet is limited. You only get the servers IP when the game wants you to get. There is not freedom besides follow the story.
10) Uplink allows you to choose which mission to make, in the sense of choosing to be a good or a bad hacker. In Hacknet some missions presentation don't have more than 2 lines. You have to accept missions without even knowing what skills you need, what tools you need and what you have to do. Its really 1 path only. And if you try to get missions in different orders you lose them, just like I lost 3. UPDATE: Because of this 1 path only + cannot accept more than 1 mission, you can game over all the time. If you delete the wrong file, edit the wrong record, its finished. People call this bug in the forum, I call this lack of flexibility. In Uplink you could simply give up on a mission and pay a fine. If you delete a file you are suppose to upload, it shouldn't be game over, just some kind of punishment.
11) It uses Unix commands but limit them. For instance you have rm command but cannot be used to delete folders. Cannot download folders either.
12) Find it a bit weird that no special software is required to know when you are being traced.
13) So far the challenge of the game seems to be more about curiosity of the player. Meaning you have to look into every folder and file and read and see what you can find (be aware) rather than having a challenge on the hacking it self, such as limited time, required software, go throught LAN networks, etc.
14) You can hack a webserver, a main frame, a home pc or a cell phone, they all look the same, they all have same file structure, they are all hacked with same tools. A bit boring no?
15) Network map completely unecessary. Its just a harder way to find servers, if you are not going to use it to bounce like Uplink, why have that? Just a window with animated blue balls. A list with a search box and some favorites would do the job, or better, connect always using the line command, IP or name assigned by the user.
16) Once you scan a server and it reveals other computers connected to that, more "balls" appears and its a mystery why some are very distant and some are very close. The distance is based on what? It simple confuses the player as it adds a connection between them and with time the connections cross each other. Well, still trying to figure out why did it this way.
17) I'm already playing this game for hours and all I do is execute programs to open ports.


The good:

a) Very well done interface in the sense that keyboard and mouse usage is well integrated. The key here is keyboard. Its very nice to be able to play the entire game using keyboard only.
b) I like the fact that webserver have website with real images. Just because its a hacker game, it doesn't mean the "normal" internet doesn't exist. Although limited, I liked the www.cfc.com.
c) You can see an effort to bring interesting content to see around. Most servers have files that are not crucial to the missions, things you can read, chats, funny stuff. That really adds to the game and was one of the things I feel lacking in Uplink. Perhaps this is one of the reason a lot of servers don't have tracing mechanism, so you don't have time pressure all the time.
d) Not having time pressure all the time is good, but also removed money pressure and other stuff, which is left it a bit unbalanced.
e) Nice animations. The screens change a lot. Its not the same interface all the time.

review_text_raw:
I have never left a review here in on steam for anything....that in itself should make you appreciate just how strongly I feel about what I am about to say and just how absolutely and unequivocally true what I am about to say really is.

Let's start from the positives.....actually positive:
The graphics are OK....along with the music it does create an atmosphere appropriate to the setting of the game.
That's it.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU BUY:
1) The game is essentially a mishap collection of dubiously formatted XML files, along with the main executable of the game which is obviously just a parser along with the graphics engine (presumably). Although it is possible to play the game normally, I guarantee that you will soon waste your time trying to "fix" the myriad of issues that arise from the poor structure of the gameplay itself (more on that later) See my play time? 87 hours? Most of it has been spent scouring the internet on ways to fix broken missions, enable progression through other parts of the story, etc.
2)There are several limits to and aspects of the basic design that make NO sense. For example, yes, you can use a "terminal" with a few commands to progress through the game. These commands include options to open and close your actual CD tray (wow, how ARG of the author--when was the last time anybody used the CD tray for anything? when was the last time anybody saw a computer with an actual CD drive ???). HOWEVER IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO CREATE OR DELETE DIRECTORIES IN YOUR IN-GAME COMPUTER, NOR CREATE FILES..That's right....as crazy as it sounds, you can't even copy files on your own machine. The only way to create files is downloading them from somewhere else and then renaming them if you want to "fake" a simple copy command....but yes, if you want a game that opens your CD tray by all means, stop reading this now and buy the game. The terminal itself has no ability to scroll up, which sometimes means you need to retrace your steps if you forgot to jot some key piece of information down.
3)There is no hardware upgrade system, which means your hacking machine is what it is from beginning to end. It doesn't really matter for the most part, as the speed of the operations you perform in the game is largely dependent on your own ability and response time (that's the main game mechanic). However RAM is kind of important, because that's what all your hacking tools consume to run, as expected. The problem is that if you, for example have the notes app open with passwords and information about your current mission (thus avoiding the aforementioned backtracking in point 2) , you will run out of memory pretty quickly...forcing you to run programs one at a time and wishing you could actually make money in this game to buy more than 1 GB of ram (lol...seriously...just lol).
4)You can only accept 1 mission at a time (WHY...JUST WHY?!???!). This may not seem a big issue, but it is what literally breaks the game again and again. This ridiculous limitation means that you can't complete all the missions offered in the game because no matter what you do as you progress through the story the game forces you to move on and leave the unfinished missions behind, never to be played. The only way to get past this is to go and edit your save game (you guessed it, an XML file) in order to make it possible to complete some missions (this fix doesn't always work btw). This becomes a huge problem close to the end of the story. Without spoiling anything, you end up having two missions to do, and it seems that it doesn't matter the order you do them in, but if you choose wrong a subsequent mission will be skipped entirely (it is one of the most notorious bugs of the game) and you will miss part of the narrative and context. Seriously, if you are thinking of buying this game, in order to enjoy the story as it was meant to be played, you should first look up what I have just told you and figure out which mission you should do first when you get to that juncture, or be prepared to restart the whole game if you mess up (unbelievable).
5)The least the author could've done was to include a save management system, but of course, there is none. If you want to make sure you don't have to restart the game in case something gets screwed up (see above) you must manually backup your savegame file, and you have to be careful too...because although the game doesn't autosave normally it will autosave in certain circumstances, barely warning you that this has been done.
6)Although the game never crashes, there are a few technical bugs that wouldn't even be a problem if not for everything that i mentioned above. When working with the terminal, using the arrow keys to edit a command sometimes doesn't work properly, and there are a few other such things (sometimes, for example, you have to hack a computer twice because although you were able to hack in the first time, the game doesn't register it). There are also a few grammar mistakes that again, not really important on its own but if added to all of the above, it's just the "cherry" on top that you don't want...especially from a paid game, however cheap it is. 
7) There is a ranking system, but it doesn't work. No matter how many missions you complete and how high your rank is according to the success emails you get at the end of each completed mission, you are still the last on the list, with 0 points. It's annoying. Suggestion to the author: if a feature is too hard/you are to lazy to implement...don't include it, especially if it has no bearing on the gameplay whatsoever. It is pretty disappointing to reach the end of the game and see that in the eyes of your hacking faction you are still a newb. 

Now....I get it, it's an indie game...what did I expect? Well I expected something a little more functional. As a software developer myself I understand a few of the choices the author made, but sill...there are some laps in basic human logic that are beyond me. For example, it is obvious that is technically more difficult to write an "open world" style game as opposed to a linear game play experience. That's why the player is allowed to play one mission at a time. I really get it. What I don't get is if a linear game is what you wanted to code...THEN DO NOT OFFER CHOICES TO THE PLAYER THAT YOUR GAME IS UNABLE TO SUPPORT AND FORCE HIM/HER/THEY TO START OVER!!!
I also understand that is hard to test a piece of software by yourself, I have done it as my main occupation for many years. A few bugs are bound to crop up...but hey...IN THE CREDITS THERE ARE MENTIONED A WHOLE SLEW OF TESTERS...what the heck did they test exactly? Seriously...I want to see what test cases they ran on this....

I would ask for a refund...but hey if didn't get my 60 bucks back from CD Projekt RED for Cyberprank 2077 I certainly won't ask the 5 bucks i spent on this (i got the DLC too). Go ahead, enjoy your Starbucks latte on me.  
According to the author, this game started out as a 48h game jam project and was later refined for 2 and a half years to become what's on steam now. 2/3 YEARS??!?!?! THIS IS WHAT YOU COME UP WITH? I think the best definition of this game is just that....a barely interesting project  hurriedly cobbled together  for a 48h game jam event.

tl;dr; Do yourself a favor and buy Uplink Elite, which is obviously what this game wanted to be and failed...miserably. I'd be willing to gift Uplink to the author as well so that he can see how a game like this SHOULD be made.

despite my playtime as of the review, ive enjoyed the game. its great! in my opinion, worth the price. sure, it has its vices, what game doesnt? the game isnt realistic to real life hacking, but i think its hard to make a game thats realistic and fun when it comes to hacking and/or programming games as it will be only for a specific audience which reduces who would play and enjoy the game by alot. its a bit repetitive with how hacking to most systems is the same, but i enjoyed many puzzles that this game provided, especially in the labyrinth DLC. this game isnt perfect, no game is but id say its honestly the closest of any games of this genre that i played. the music is one of the few game soundtracks that i actually liked and would listen to in my spare time. the multiple times that arent just port openers are fun and useful!... well most of them (looking at you, Clock.exe). but id say that some are underused, like the log creator and opener, theyre required to be used i think 2-3 times, but the gap between their uses is too big which makes those tools easily forgettable and can make some puzzles hard to impossible without googling how to solve them. id also say that the [b][h1]I almost wanted to write this as a negative review.[/h1][/b]
However, on balance, I switched the direction of that thumb.

Full disclosure: I am a professional sysadmin, and I Tux and I are old buddies. He didn't like me at first, but I pulled his source and patched it, and now he [b]loves[/b] me. 

[h1] First the things that drove me up the wall...[/h1]

Mostly, it was the [b]almost[/b] unix commands, like 'RM *' instead of 'rm -r -f' and things like supporting tab completion and wildcards but [i]not[/i] partial names [i]with[/i] wildcards. I can't tell you how many times muscle memory had me type 'RM @32[Tab]*' to delete all logs that began with @3213 - but this does [i]not[/i] work in-game. You either delete everything, or have to type in each file one at a time. Fortunately, this ultimately proved irrelevant after I later discovered all other in-game admins use their keyboards only as a protective drool mat for their desks (more on that below.)

Also, the fact that you could just RM * and expect that the sysadmin on the system wouldnot find it suspicious at all that the system lacks logs of any kind for a whole time perod, and the last log is a x.x.x.x disconnected with no matching 'connected' message. Nope. Nothing suspicious there.

Almost makes me ashamed of wearing a white hat in real life. 

[h1]Kudos to the devs to for trying to acquaint us with RFC1700, but...[/h1]

What I found silly and pointless was to use real port numbers that you'd exepct to see in real life servers (22 for ssh, etc) but making you type in the port numbers for your magic 'sploit to work against (where there is never any deviation [i][b]ever[/b][/i] from the standard) is just silly as well.

[i]Note: I guess the IANA in-game must have been OK with that company creating the protocol that uses port 104, as that is in the range of ports they control assignments for... Just sayin' [/i]

I would assume a hacker as talented as 'bit' that could write a magic rootkit could figure out that if I didn't provide a port number for an SSH exploit, that it should just assume something as reasonable as, oh... assuming that the ssh daemon is running on port 22 like every. single. system. in the game's universe.

[h1]Word to the devs: It's either 'magic' hacking, or it's realistic. Pick your direction and don't try to do both at once.[/h1]

I guess my complaints kind of revolved around the fence sitting. Why go to all that trouble to get many technical details right, but still use hacking tools that so advanced as to appear 'magic' but at the same time retarded in so many easily fixed ways.

They even showed enough 'nix savvy to use tools like ps and kill mostly accurately and to cleverly make 'nmap' the command to trigger a scan for listening ports.

[b]Ironically, I guess that proves Bit's programming skills are a bit hit or miss (pun intended.)[/b] He did make nmap not require all its real-life complicated arguments and just assume you were doing an active port scan against the host you were connected to.

Those kind of professional pedantic nitpicks are why I wanted so badly to make this a negative review.

But not everyone is a professional sysadmin, and probably wouldn't have known or cared because they don't know better.

[h1]I am forced to admit, though...[/h1]
It's actually a very fun game. I applaud them for trying so hard to simulate the use of the command line where real sysadmins work. I also applaud them for at least trying to make people aware of the principles of security (or insecurity, as it were.)

I think it was worth the money. Nobody that doesn't live in my professional circles would be bothered by things like not being able to cd from one subdirectory directly to another because the GUI is so much easier and more convenient for this anyway.

If they would just have fixed the parser to accept partial wildcards and made the opposing sysadmins not complete clowns, I would have enjoyed it more.

On balance: 8/10 would be frustrated by the lack of being able to chain 'CD /logs && RM * && dc'  all over again.

UPDATE - A couple of days after I post this review, the developer announces that he patched the bug that made the game impossible to complete. While another bug does exist at present (where if you do not accept the Junebug mission in time, you lose the opportunity to continue with the main story), it is possible to work around this by reloading an old save.

Upon reaching the end of the game, I am absolutely convinced that this game is one of (if not) the best hacking simulators on the market. The final mission in the game is so intense. I had to do it in several parts and my heart was racing each time I started it. There was nothing I could suggest to make the gameplay itself any better. Maybe adding in more missions to give it some replayability and a bit more freedom to go off and hack to your hearts content for good or for evil. However, that could be a DLC pack and can easily be added in. As the game stands, it deserves an 8/10, purely because it's still not perfect in terms of the bugs. However, they should be fixed soon given the dedication the dev has with this game.

- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

Let me be perfectly clear with this before you read any further. I LOVE Hacknet. It's a fantastic game and is definitely better than Uplink by a mile. The use of real computer commands makes it feel much more realistic and the storyline is pretty awesome to boot. Plus, the time limit you have when a trace counter starts rapidly going down and you're waiting for the password crack to finish so you can intercept the trace creates one heck of an adrenaline rush.

However I cannot recommend it as it is now. There is a single bug I have encountered that makes the game impossible to complete. I will try to avoid giving away any spoilers, so this will be a bit vague. Later in game you are required to take on a mission that is part of the main storyline. However, you do not choose when this mission comes to you. It is automatically sent to you in an email and I'm not 100% sure what the criteria is for it appearing. To complete it, you need an .exe file used to crack a specific port which is only available by taking on a side mission. However, this mission is locked and once again, I do not know what the criteria is to unlock it. So I tried to take on the other available missions in an attempt to unlock the one I needed. In order to do this, you must abort the main storyline mission. Aborting a mission means you can NEVER attempt it again, making it impossible to continue with the main storyline. While I discovered it is possible to obtain the .exe without the mission, following an online walkthrough to obtain the information needed to get it instead of getting it in game feels wrong on so many levels, especially since it's deeply hidden within this seemingly permanently locked mission.

So at this time, I can't recommend it. The game is good, but I haven't been able to finish it because of this bug. The developer seems to be quite willing to take feedback and work on it so if you're reading this, I eagerly await a patch for this game. I can't wait to finish it.

[h1]WARNING this review will have spoilers, however, I've already marked what I consider to be spoilers[/h1]

This review is [b]NOT[/b] for people who plan on going through this game and only doing what the scripts you to. This is for those who want to delete everything they can get into after downloading files that they'd like to save as trophies or blackmail.

This is a great game, I have yet to beat it but I've loved most of the time I've put into this game, which is why I'm sad to say that I can't recommend this game. My main issue with it is the fact that its dead, unless I'm mistaken which is very possible. This game is filled with hand placed text and files as well as scripted events. At one point in the game, towards the beginning, [spoiler]you have to hack into a clicker game (that you can actually play which is super cool!) in order to delete an elite player's save so that he can show off his clicker power once more! I deleted the entire game alongside EVERYONE's saves. If you choose to do this you don't need to fret, you can still play the game, which is the main issue... WHY CAN I PLAY A DELETED GAME?[/spoiler] This trend follows with pretty much any computer or server you hack into, no one reacts, nothing gets repaired over time and things still work... WHY? Why does no one care if I've deleted ALL their system files, why do things still work even after I've deleted the file that basically says "DO NOT DELETE OR WILL STOP WORKING!!!" And why can't I blackmail people? I probably won't be able to get myself to beat this game because it just feels dead to me, sure its a lot of fun, but the immersion is killed the second I try to jump ship and do my own thing.

A second issue some people may have with this game is that it expects you to know, or figure out, everything outside of the few basic things it teachs you from the start, sometimes while being put under the clock. I have no real gripes with this, the game doesn't hold your hand (which I like), the only reason I mentioned it was for those players who don't like being forced to figure out solutions they've never been taught.

tl;dr: This game is dead, do anything outside of the script and its like nothing happened and no one cares. Make sure you can think on your feet and make sure you don't mind finding solutions to problems you've never even seen before.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What to expect if you're new to this game genre[/h1]
Hacknet is a new title in the otherwise stagnant, indie genre of hacking simulation games.
And a fresh breeze it is.

No doubt there is hardly any competition for this kind of quality.
Graphics are amazing, the hacking system introduced is quite good and consistent, it has gigantic potential for expansion that desperately needs to be used, and hopefully will. In it's current shape there might be little room for multiplayer gameplay, because of the game mechanics, but hopefully as the game gets finalized it will be implemented.

The puzzles you have to face are fun to solve and most of the time at medium or easy difficulty level.
Even though the game description provided on Steam might be a little misleading, as to non-holywood hacking style, or minimal hand-holding, the gameplay can be extremely exciting and satisfying.
The thrill of hacking, taking unauthorised control over websites, other web services, or user machines and mobile devices, identity theft or destruction, and constantly racing the trace clock are all very satisfying and will give you an addictive adrenaline rush.

Music is a very proper and enjoyable background for your virtual crimes, not quite something to remember.

The game has too high hardware requirements in my opinion. All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!)

[h1]Finally the 'Uplink vs Hacknet'[/h1]
Many people look up to Hacknet in comparison to Uplink.
Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy.
The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging.
If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding.
Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet.

[h1]Final words[/h1]
Whatever Hacknet is or will be, I'd say Uplink is worth playing, as the only other hacking game out there with some serious gameplay to this date.
If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers.
Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

The puzzles you have to face are fun to solve and most of the time at medium or easy difficulty level. Even though the game description provided on Steam might be a little misleading, as to non-holywood hacking style, or minimal hand-holding, the gameplay can be extremely exciting and satisfying. The thrill of hacking, taking unauthorised control over websites, other web services, or user machines and mobile devices, identity theft or destruction, and constantly racing the trace clock are all very satisfying and will give you an addictive adrenaline rush. Music is a very proper and enjoyable background for your virtual crimes, not quite something to remember. The game has too high hardware requirements in my opinion. All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!) Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy. The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging. If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding. Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet. [h1]Final words[/h1] Whatever Hacknet is or will be, I'd say Uplink is worth playing, as the only other hacking game out there with some serious gameplay to this date. If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers. Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

[h1][b]IF YOU LIKE THE IDEA OF A GAME FOCUSING ENTIRELY ON A TERMINAL/COMMAND-LINE AND SOME EASY TO MODERATELY DIFFICULT PUZZLES THROWN IN, YOU MAY LIKE THIS GAME.[/b][/h1]
As someone who has a bit of experience with the UNIX terminal and commands, this game had my absolute full attention and felt familiar to me. [b]I've just recently bought this game (yesterday, at the time of writing) and I was absolutely HOOKED and couldn't get away from it. Hacknet is absolutely my style of game! (right now, I've just beaten the base game and will go through the DLC content shortly. but I may fiddle around with the Extensions)[/b]

[h1][b]TARGET[/b][/h1]
Obviously, this game isn't for everyone. A terminal-based game can seem intimidating or uninteresting to someone who has no experience with it before (and even if you do, a terminal-based game may not be that interesting). If the screenshots and description provided by the game do not capture your attention, it's probably not the game for you. But if your curiosity is piqued, it may be a great experience for you.

[h1][b]PUZZLE ELEMENTS AND TUTORIALS[/b][/h1]
Hacknet introduces itself quite well to the uninformed, and doesn't hand-hold. It throws you straight in after a short tutorial on using the terminal and interface, therefore encouraging experimentation with what you have available. By not holding the player's hand, succeeding in the puzzles without any additional help besides what the game provides will give you a sense of accomplishment. However, that can turn some people off, and if it does, it may not be for you.

It is possible to get stuck in several points in the game, but no solution is too far out there and is solvable without a walkthrough. (and I admit, I have, and have consulted a walkthrough but I was extra careful not to look any further ahead than the current task at hand, most of the time I had just forgotten something simple and was able to get back on track quickly).

The puzzles start off pretty easy, leading you on and increasing the difficulty as it goes, pretty much gently guiding you on how to work with the game's unique nature.

At certain times, the tasks can seem repetitive, and to be fair, it is. You are constantly trying to break into a lot of different computers, servers, devices, etc. but that's what it is. It is an accurate representation instead of the flashy Hollywood style hacking seen on film (but it certainly can be flashy when it wants to be and is for certain parts).

[h1][b]STORY[/b][/h1]
The story itself is nothing outstanding, but it certainly fits the theme and style of the game. It's perfect for the game. The story is there for the beginning and the end of your gameplay, giving you purpose to start and an objective to reach near the end. In the middle of the game, you are given freedom to do what you wish. Or PointClicker, if that's your thing (I won't judge!).

[h1][b]MUSIC[/b][/h1]
The music is an absolute fit for Hacknet and I often found myself focusing on the killer beats rather than what's at hand. It also made me quite shaky during the parts that are time-based.

[h1][b]OVERALL[/b][/h1]
Overall, Hacknet is extremely accurate compared to other things that have tried to display this kind of topic before. The elements work wonderfully and the balance between gameplay and the real elements is on point (all the commands given are used at one point or another and no unnecessary garbage is there). To the average person who may not know anything about the terminal, it can be exciting to get into it for the first time not knowing anything and eventually learn (there may be a little higher risk of getting stuck at a point, but that's okay!). To those who are a little familiar with the terminal and commands, you'll feel right at home and understand the game quickly and have a great time with it!

[h1][b]SHOULD YOU GET IT?[/b][/h1]
If this game looks interesting, [b]IT WILL BE FOR YOU.[/b] The terminal looks intimidating from the start, and if that doesn't deter you and the description of the game brings you in further, you [b]WILL[/b] enjoy it!

review_text_raw:
A very introspective look at UNIX commands and the general actions of hacking - which is basically accurate, but taking out the time required to accomplish these things (for example, you can solve port protocols within a few seconds, but IRL this might take hours).

Basically, if you want the "reality" where you are the hacker in one of these movies (you're not playing the hacker, but ARE the hacker), then this is pretty spot-on. It just removes most of the tedium of the acitivites. This is not to say that the game isn't repetitive; it is, and remains true to its roots as a simulator. By nature, most simulators run off of repetitive actions which require muscle memory and timing in order to complete.

In actual fact, this is more of a puzzle-solving game. However, combined with some funny easter eggs (IRC chats can get hilarious) and honest-to-god methodology on the principles of hacking, this actually becomes enjoyable unless you just want to shoot things in the face (in which case, this is NOT the game for you).

Anyone who wants to work in software QA should be able to play this game comfortably, figure out most of the puzzles, and genuinely enjoy the experience. If you can't, don't take QA as a career. Because this in almost any form is what you do - all day, every day. I know this from 14 years of experience at that job in everything from game development to SAS or security software.

There are a few points I wish there were more of, or more developed. As game, it's pretty linear. There are nice little things like finding additional information on a server which gives you another terminal to hack, or a phone to break into, but these are too few and far between. It could be far more sandboxy if there were a freeform mode for points, which had sets of systems and connected devices which would allow you to randonly investigate things you found on another system. In this, you'd need a points system or something to gain (money, cred, whatever) - which would be a welcome addition to the game. I think another fun mode would be to actually use the system specs for the computer it was running on for memory, etc. as well as randonly generating in-game groups to become involved with, do missions for (from forums, etc.)

I recommend this game, just due to the simulation nature being captured very well. That being said, this game won't be for everyone. Much of the game is tedium and random investigation - which is exactly what hacking is about. One of the best missions which represents this is the "Project Junebug" mission. You're basically let loose to figure out how to accomlish the task, you have a lot of reading to do to catch up on how to accomplish it, and there isn't any handholding. YOU have to do the tasks, to the best of your understanding, and figure out indeed, what those tasks are, and it involves multiple servers, and different methods of having the same outcome.

I have been waiting for the game to start, and now that I'm halfway through I've given up. It's boring and pointless. There is no story, there are no choices (even though the game wants you to think there are). That aside, it's not really a hacking game. "Hacking" just means typing the same commands and waiting for them to execute... every time... for every PC in the network.

Another big problem is that the game implies that it will use real world logic but then it doesn't. Like I can't execute a file on a PC I'm connected to? Since when? 

Instructions are never clear and even if they are I hate that the game forces me to only do things how the dev intended. Specifically for advcancing missions, it's never clear whether I just need to read the file or send it or send the password contained in it. All of those should work, not just one!

There are bugs - mostly soft locks, which is unacceptable for such a simple game.

Instead of spending time on the visualizations for each tool the dev should have spent time designing mechanics around them. For instance the firewall analyzer is okay. Not fun, but it's not completely idle, you have to do something. Each tool has to be like that, there has to be some mini-game associated with it, or there has to be some strategy as to which tools are used in what order.

I don't know what the music was like. It was so repeptitve so annoying I turned it off and played Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines OST. 

The only thing I liked about the game is the environmental storytelling. The chat logs sound EXACTLY like the Old Internet days. Kudos to the author for the research!

review_text_raw:
[+] Soundtrack
[+] User Interface

[-] Plot
[-] World design and interaction

I bought this game mainly for its soundtrack, then because I'm a terminal guy myself and I love typing commands.
From this standpoint the game is beautiful: hastily keyboard mashing while listening to Gallego's killer tracks was awesome, not even mentioning the time when Carpenter Brut took over...

This game perfectly sets the mood for an awesome experience, with its music, its terminals and pseudo-graphical GUIs... but then falls short story-side.

[b]The plot is dull, linear and somewhat predictable.[/b]
You only have one bifurcation of the storyline that's even non-obvious to unlock. It gives you access to some more interesting missions, a new faction, and let you see a dark corner of the in-game Internet; but then it merges back into the main path in an abrupt way, as meaningless as it could get.
Yes, there are some interesting easter eggs and strange computer systems, but nothing that makes you want to explore on your own all that much.
There's only, like, [i]one[/i] moral choice, and it's not even part of the main quest.

[b]Whatever you do, whoever you damage, there's no consequence. The world simply doesn't react.[/b]
No cops backtracing you, no factions you can anger, no reputation system: you're part of the Good Guys from start to finish; you can screw up all the machines you want, you are The Savior and no one will change that.
Heck, you can even fail hacks and, apart from a panicking minigame to atone, no officer nor corporate killer will ever knock on your door.
You're simply bounced from a Good faction to another, without any chance to express your will. Just keep on hacking. Don't even bother to cover up your footprints. Logs are useless.

In the end, yes you can buy it, sure, but don't expect much except aesthetics.


[TECHNICAL NOTE]
The in-game console is backed by your native OS, and everything is deeply woven with its runtime.
Yes, you read it right.
That means two things:
[list]
    [*] if some of your game files break, you can be welcomed by an OS error printed on the console;
    [*] while this game runs on both Windows and Linux and has cloud sync, the save files are [b]not[/b] cross-platform; I suspect it has to do with different text encodings (save files are simple XMLs), and you need a repair tool you can find on the forums in order to convert them.
[/list]
Yeah, that wasn't nice.

review_text_raw:
Lemme start by saying that this feels like it'd be a pretty niche title.  If the idea of entering commands into a terminal and making notes about IP addresses and passwords does not appeal to you, then turn away now since that's the majority of the gameplay here.


Hacknet fits into the very, very tiny genre of hacking games.  No, not Watch Dogs.  More like Uplink.  And... umm... others?  I honestly don't know of any other titles in this genre, to be honest!  It's a game about breaking into servers, looking for information, and then covering your tracks.  As the game progresses, you'll be tested on your ability to type accurately, multi-task quickly, and ability to dig deep for details in order to progress.  It's a satisfying experience, but I can see where this can get incredibly frustrating, or boring, for some.

Note:  I do not own the DLC and, therefore, it does not factor into this review.

The Good

-Somewhat simulates Real Life™ hacking, versus the "Hollywood" hacking used in Uplink.  It's cool, but I imagine its very simplied and toned down.  But, it's still really neat.

-Makes a fairly daunting premise pretty easy to figure out and play.  The tutorials explain things well enough and stuff isn't thrown at you too fast.  You won't get turned loose on your own until you have a firm grasp of things and you'll never get in over your head.

-Meanwhile, the game is still challenging enough you'll have to stop and think things through at times or get put into situations where the pressure is on and you can't afford to make mistakes.  

-Good music.  It's not great music, persay, but it sets the mood well and isn't distracting.  Not something I'd plan on listening to out of the game, but I definitely appreciate its presence.

-Workshop support is always a good thing to have in a game.  I've not tried the stuff out yet, but it seems like people can do things like add new missions and stuff, which is cool and can add a lot of longevity to the game.


The Neutral

-The plot...  its serviceable, but a bit predictable.  Kinda a shrug rating.


The Bad

Steam needs to update the rating system. This thumbs up/down is just too simplistic. While I do recommend the game for those who never played a hack "sim" before, I get the feeling that some people who are used to Uplink will be disappointed.

Uplink is the only game like this one I've played, and Hacknet is obviously inspired by it, so this is basically a comparison between the 2.

If you played Uplink this will be a walk in the park. Aside from visuals, there's nothing here that Uplink didn't do better back in 2001. With the excepton of a couple of moments, all missions are exactly the same all the way through, so it gets repetitive quite fast. 

There's no sense of danger or urgency Uplink gives you. Nobody will come after you, there's no police, companies you hack won't give a shit. Despite of what the game tells you right at the beggining, there's no need to cover your tracks. In Uplink, everytime you hack into a system it's a race against time. In Hacknet there's nothing like it. Once you block a trace you can spend as much time as you want in any system.

There's no rig upgrades, no rewards, nothing like it. You just complete the mission, get a "thank you" email and move on to the next.  

Both games have a story, but Uplink is more of a sandbox. After you get the hang of it you can do whatever you want and follow the story whenever you want. Hacknet, on the other hand, is pretty linear. That's a big dissapointment, specially after a great "wtf do I do now" moment right in the beggining. After that, you get the feeling you're never safe, but unfortunately nothing like that ever happens again. Storywise, Uplink is way more interesting, while Hacknet is cliche and way too simplistic.

That's the main problem with this game. It's way too easy. Uplink is infuriating unforgiven to the player. Once you start to mess with big companies, one small screw up means game over. Add that to the fact that the game is pretty much a roguelike, so it's not like you can go back to a previous save, you have to start all over again. In Hacknet, you don't need to worry about that. Like I said before, there's no need to clean after you. If you get caught, all you need to do is change your ip adress.

Anyway, if you never played a hacking "sim" before, this might be a good place to start. Like Uplink, It's really easy to get into, you don't need to now anything about code to play both games, and they give you a good sense of immersion.   

Hacknet has a good concept, but is way too simple for those looking for a challenge. I hope the "Labyrinths" expansion adds more substance to the game.

5/10

Got the game for free and it has been sitting in my backlog for a while. Some while ago I finally decided to clear this game with high expectations seeing it receive a lot of positive reviews. Unfortunately I was faced with only disappointment.

At first the gameplay is intriguing and engaging. The terminal style UI certainly looks cool. There are quests that procedurally guide you through the mechanics of the game, and the discovery process keeps the gameplay fresh, but not for long until you join the hacker organization.

From that point what you do is just repeating the same hacking routine again and again, and it gets repetitive very quickly. At this point the only thing left that can do some good for this game is the story. My last hope for the game was that after hours of labour I would uncover traces of a big conspiracy that leads me to something like stopping a skynet, or fighting myself in a moral conflict, you get the meaning.

But no! The main plot is linear and doesn't have much depth to it. It was so uninspiring that I didn't even know I came to the end of the story, just after I did the usual hacking stuff I was greeted with a voice recording and I was like "is that it?".

Also the 'hacking experience' is far from realistic. But I guess it serves the point of letting people feel like they're a hacker.

I really want to like this game, but I couldn't. The music is good though, I think it's the only plus side.

TL;DR: Cool hacking-look UI, repetitive hacking routine, weak story

[b]A HACKER GROUP SEARCHING THE TRUTH[/b]
[i]Hacknet[/i] was available for free in Humble Bundle for a short period, long time ago. It's one of those game that normally I wouldn't buy. The game is centered on group of hackers that receives some contracts from people that wants to obtain something: it could be retrieving a file or cancel something from another user computer. For the entire game, you will see the Hacknet OS, a system that allows to execute some tools and let you inside other networks and devices.

[h1]VERY REPETITIVE GAMEPLAY[/h1]
At the beginning [i]Hacknet[/i] seems promising. The game make you feel like you are a real hacker, trying to break in other people computers, but after a while everything repeat itself. You always do the same things: hack devices ports, with specific executables that you just need to download from the hacker group server, once you are in, you need to check the files, and once you completed the task, simply reply to the client request mail, with details needed. Some of these contract are challenging and it will take a lot of time, trying to understand which is the solution of the enigma. Usually there is not only one way to go, but you can complete the mission in different ways. The real problem is that missions are all the same and nothing really change for the whole game.

[h1]CANCEL THE LOGS[/h1]
One of the things that the game never stop to stress you out is deleting the logs in a computer after you finished to snoop around. At the beginning I did it, because I was scared that I could be traced, losing the mission. After a while, because you have so many steps to do in order to complete the contract, I forgot to clean them several times, and nothing happened. They cannot trace me so I simply stopped to worry about it: I canceled only when I remembered.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
[i]Hacknet[/i] could have potential. It looks different and interesting, but, as I've mentioned before, you need to do always the same bunch of actions, and this made me lose the interest in the game. I have still to complete the main story, but I think I played enough to express an opinion on this title. I really wanted to buy also DLCs, but after this experience, I think I stop here my experience with this game.

review_text_raw:
There are clear influences from Uplink, but Hacknet stands on its own two feet for many design decisions.

Hacknet requires a lot of typing due to the text console. This brings a level of realism which is enjoyable, and the countdown timers do not seem to require the player to type at 200 words per minute. However, a few actions can also be initiated by mouse using a graphical user interface. The use of the mouse is a bit incoherent: those features which can use the mouse and those which cannot feel arbitrary and without obvious design merit.

There are a number of little bugs here and there. Head over to the discussions and check the bug report thread. Many of the valid bugs reported actually have more to do with polish. It's unfair to call them bugs, but fixing the issues could enhance the game's polish and lead to better immersion. There are a few actual bugs that can lead to gameplay issues, but they seem to be few and far between.

The story is a bit linear. I have found it hard to explore the networked universe outside where the missions take me. Compare this to Uplink, where there are a great many ways to find and access computers by goofing around. Computers tend to have random snippets from bash.org , which are humorous logs of conversations that reportedly happened on IRC. It's a nice touch as a reward for looking at systems and it makes them feel a little more fleshed out, yet the contents tend to be disconnected from any of the game's context. The snippets simultaneously help and hurt immersion.

Creative expression is available in small doses, but I do not consider this any kind of sandbox game. The potential for such a thing is there. For example, there are computers which run web servers. You can modify the HTML, and when you visit the web server, your changes are visible. It can be amusing to deface a virtual server even if no other living being will see it. However, if you delete all the system files from a computer and then forcibly shut it down, it should prevent the system from rebooting. This would destroy a system. In Hacknet, if you do this, the system will disappear from your network map for a little while and then come back (while still lacking system files). As a related polish-bug: you can immediately connect to any computer "destroyed" this way using the command console, even if the network map does not show the system as online.

The music is electronica-themed to suit the stereotype of a computer hacker. The sound track brings good ambience. I personally start to notice the repetitious nature of the music after playing 2-3 solid hours, but that's usually a good time to take a break anyway.

The recent release for Linux/Mac is welcome, except that has introduced a number of new bugs that need to be squashed. Save game interoperability is a current problem that needs to be resolved at the time of this writing. Linux/Mac support has its own thread in the game's Steam discussion area. I'm sure those problems will be resolved soon enough, but they are worth reading through before purchasing if you plan to play on Mac or Linux.

Overall, I'd say Hacknet is a fun puzzle game with a solid computer hacker theme. It could use more polish and the design decisions regarding keyboard or mouse interfacing could use some rethinking. As a professional programmer and IT person, I cannot really say with certainty if this game is accessible to non-programmers or non-IT people. I suspect the game is approachable enough to anyone who has ever had to type commands into anything instead of clicking glittery UI buttons.

review_text_raw:
This game is about hacking as the name implies, starting you off with a bare few programs and growing your arsenal as you progress its storyline. This game stands as a spiritual successor to Uplink bar a few features that keep it from reaching Uplink's cult following, but still make the game interesting and make me wish the two games had merged into one supergame with the visuals of Hacknet and the in-depth sandbox nature of Uplink.

Starting with a bootup sequence, an automated message box by the "Bit" character and a tutorial program with a cool digital background soundtrack sets the tone for the game immediately. Given basic instructions to hack your first terminal can take time to figure out even with the tutorials. Learning these commands will be the bread and butter of this game, and so with every successful command you'll be rewarded with a visual representation of the program functioning to unlock ports or simply find a password.

This game doesn't rely on money for upgrades, and in turn missions do not give money but instead increases your rank. Increasing your rank will allow you bigger missions, and will grant you access to servers to download more powerful programs which will allow you to crack more secure servers and reveal that the missions lead a linear path with admittedly little room to shift the way the story goes.

Like Uplink, this can be a very short and very easy game to get through if you know what you're doing. This is made easier with the ability to save and the Trace Aversion game, should you lag behind or stay on a server while being traced and run out of time. The Trace Aversion sequence isn't anything special in terms of gameplay, but you will be given a timelimit to hack a server and type in your IP address to avert a game over, requiring a few midgame tools at the least.

I've yet to finish the game, and I've recently gotten stuck at a point where I require a program from another mission before I can finish my current mission. I'd advise doing everything you can before starting the endgame, because there's some programs hidden behind locked missions waiting for you to reach the top rank before allowing you to take them, these missions hold programs that are required for the end game. There's also a few guides available for the little confusing things, in which they are in abundance.

Overall I do like what I've seen, and there's definitely a charming nature that comes from these hacking games with Hacknet being no different. I'd recommend it for anyone interested in simulations, puzzles, and anyone who just likes to solve things on their own. This is Hollywood hacking at its core though, and it doesn't represent real techniques used by actual hackers.

Hacknet is the lone developer's pet project, and it saddens me to give it a negative rating. Honestly, though, I just didn't enjoy the game at all. It is extraordinarily repetitive, and after a while, it feels that you're doing nothing except waiting for hacking animations to finish. With only 2 exceptions, [i] every [/i] mission can be beaten by typing the same 6-7 commands in a predetermined order. After 2-3 hours of gameplay, I kept asking myself, "why is every mission the same, and why am I being forced to do it again and again?"

I did enjoy the jokes hidden in the IRC chat logs, but even then, they repeated themselves. If you read every IRC log in the game, you'd run across the same exact joke (literally) 4-5 times. It's a bit disappointing that the developer couldn't even populate the IRC logs with unique jokes. 

As an alternative criticism... the UI has some definite issues. For example, the node map gets so cluttered that it becomes completely unusable. You're constantly forced to backtrack and look at the mission statement in order to remind yourself which nodes should be broken into. It's very frustrating, and definitely killed my sense of immersion.

All in all, I can't recommend this game. I understand that others love it, but honestly, it just wasn't for me.

With only 2 exceptions, [i] every [/i] mission can be beaten by typing the same 6-7 commands in a predetermined order. After 2-3 hours of gameplay, I kept asking myself, "why is every mission the same, and why am I being forced to do it again and again?" I did enjoy the jokes hidden in the IRC chat logs, but even then, they repeated themselves. If you read every IRC log in the game, you'd run across the same exact joke (literally) 4-5 times. It's a bit disappointing that the developer couldn't even populate the IRC logs with unique jokes. As an alternative criticism... the UI has some definite issues. For example, the node map gets so cluttered that it becomes completely unusable. You're constantly forced to backtrack and look at the mission statement in order to remind yourself which nodes should be broken into. It's very frustrating, and definitely killed my sense of immersion. All in all, I can't recommend this game. I understand that others love it, but honestly, it just wasn't for me.
