review_text_raw:
Shall..we..play..a..game?

Welcome to Hacknet, a game that made me feel so much that i was somewhere inside a 80's hacker movie it had me waiting for Joshua to call me to tell me we needed to finish the game we started.

I was really surprised at how much i enjoyed the game being that it is mostly text based but to the details.

The game is niche but even if you have only the most basic and i mean BASIC keyboarding skills you can quickly get the commands down. If you've ever set up your own linux box and just messed around with it a little bit you can play this game. If you watched Wargames, Hackers, Ghost in the Shell, or played Cyberpunk, Shadowrun, or Anarchy Online you will want to play this game. I picked it up during a 75% off sale and only now started playing and it is very addicting and hilarious at the same time. There are some parts that really screw with your mind and so as not to spoil the story let me just say that you must "role play" the persona in the game. When the things that screw with your mind happen you have to ask yourself "What would my "Hacker" persona do?"

The soundtrack is very techno-club and adds to the overall feel of the game nicely.
The learning curve is a bit like a roller coaster and if you aren't paying attention you can find yourself stuck and wondering what to do.

You won't learn to code, or "hack", or script anything. You will get really good practice at some few basic Linux commands in the terminal which is good practice and fun. I haven't found a binary compiler in the game so haven't been able to figure out what the binary code files are or if i'm even supposed to figure out what they are. but it's still fun to wonder.

This game has great multi-player potential but other reviews indicate that the developers may not do any more with it. Also there is no multi-monitor support which would be a really nice touch but isn't likely to happen either.

I've put almost 5 hours at this point; found a bunch of stuff; lost a bunch of stuff; got my stuff back and loved every minute of it. The game won't teach you to be a hacker, but it is the Hacking game you didn't know that you desperately needed to play.

It is a niche game to be sure but if you are feeling a bit nostalgic after the gaming references i've made, download the game and enjoy. I did buy it on very cheap sale, 75% off,  but $10 isn't an excessive price point for a really fun game. I don't see a whole lot of replaying the game due to the linear storyline. Steam community has added some content and there seems to be enough material from the community to make the game worthwhile.


*SPOILER ALERT*

No matter WHAT happens, always rember:

help
help 2
help 3

The ability to move forward in the game is usually found in those tools. If you are stuck, study the "help" pages.

review_text_raw:
TLDR: Do you want to pretend you're a hacker while listening to coding music? Well, this is probably the closest thing to it, and you can actually have some fun while doing it! Get your bearings in a similar to Unix coding interface with simple and straightforward instructions from clients and other friendly hackers, then take contracts with various objectives ranging from modifying files to remotely (maybe?) stopping a man's heart.

Story: As an unknown protagonist, take on a pretty big security threat towards freedom of the people, a final request from a person named Bit. Try your best to learn how to overcome various security obstacles ranging from firewalls to encrypted files by obtaining data and programs from lesser guarded PCs and servers.

Gameplay: This is 90% typing and looks a lot more complicated than it really is. When you really think about it, there's very little gameplay going on and little content. However, you will have eureka moments and THAT is where the meat of the game was to me. I enjoyed the hell out of it and beat myself over the head by not using a guide. Which explains my many hours on the game, as I often hit a roadblock and would just start a new game a few weeks later (it ended up being a few years later as I just beat it in 2025).
The majority of the game consists of downloading programs from various sources to be able to use them against better protected machines that you need access to, to complete whatever objective you currently have. 
It can become easy to hit a roadblock. Thankfully, there's a help window and auto complete key that helps you speed things along and allows some wiggling room in your typing. It is not going to hold your hand, however, and the fact that the game feels like a giant puzzle, or I should say an ever increasing series of hurdles to get over will not fancy everyone. 
Well, I loved it, I'm a masochist, bring it on.

Graphics: This is really just coding with a nice UI and some effects on the side to keep things... lively.

Audio: If you're playing with only one screen and you get a blue screen of death, it's scary. It's spot on. The tracks are few but fitting and nice.

I'm still dumb after playing this but at least... I finally beat it! On an unrelated note, I had fun opening and closing my cd tray within the game. It's that weird of an experience.

review_text_raw:
Well, a fter a 9 hours journey in the world of virtual hacking, I must say I'm satisfied but also a bit sad it was so short. 

At first, I thought it would be a needlessly complicated and boring game but I decided to give it a chance and, boy did I make the right decision. The game was complex enough that anybody without basic computer skills wouldn't stand a chance against this game but it's simplified enough that you don't have to remember dozens of complex commands, you can easily complete a command by pressing TAB, which makes the games less of a chore.

The story is engaging as the death of a known hacker named Bit is slowly revealed to be not a fruit of some accident but something more sinister and you are his last hope of successfully executing plans that might be the difference between corporate digital control and freedom. Along the way, there are contracts to fulfill, ranging from simple information retrieval to adding or removing entries from a death row record and even hacking a suffering patient's pacemaker to give its host a peaceful, painless death. And as you progress, you'll find programs that will help you get inside more secure systems in order to complete the more difficult contracts.

The game is not devoid of humor as you'll find IRC chat logs and other documents inside the devices you hack and some of them are hilarious, such as a guy replacing the word "wand" with "wang" in the first Harry Potter book and has posted some excerpts that are good for a laugh or a guy telling how he stood in front of his nerighbour's burning house, holding a stick with a marshmallow.

The sad thing with these files is they're lacking in variety and often you'll find the same files on different computer, breaking the impression that beyong the machines you're hacking, there are people going about their everyday lives and chatting about different aspects of their lives. As entertaining as they are, once you've read these logs, there's not really anything else worth reading.

Hacknet is pretty linear and all the paths you can take bring you to the same ending. One of the things I found disappointing is, you're never really in much danger, except once, when some other hacked decides to attack you, deleting your UI and forcing you to get out of this mess through terminal. It was a tense moment where I wanted to get back at the guy but none of what I did made the slight difference and once you get out of this mess, there are no other instance where you have to fight off other hackers.

Overall this was a great experience and I would love to play a sequel or at least, an extension, I hope the developper will give us more Hacknet and expand upon all the ideas that were implemented. I wholeheartedly recommend this game for those who like smart, logical experiences and detective games.

$> connect `gethostbyname Steam`
$> cd /Hacknet/Reviews
$> getString Review

Truly amazing game, funny, engaging, and for all types of people who like to solve mysteries and logical puzzles. The story mode can be done under 10 hours, but the game deserves 100% its price.

If you do not have experience in networking, or using computers from command line at all, do not fear. The game introduces you into it gradually and you'll get the trick of it in no time.

If you do (like myself) have experience in networking, or using computers from command line, do not fear either. It feels real, familiar (Unix-like shell), but the "gradually introducing you" is not spoonfeeding you with "type XY to do Z" kind of pop-ups that annoy you. The game has several things "of its own" that you will learn really fast and I saw myself really excited and feeling like I was exploring some kind of distro like BackTrack or Kali Linux and going like "look at the amount of tools we've got!! And they work like a charm, too!"
If you are not a real-life hacker, you'll sure feel like one in here.

I followed the role of a white hat (it aligns with my way of thinking), although some of my in-game actions could qualify enough to be considered "grey". The good thing here is that you have complete freedom to approach and follow the story filling your own role, without the game forcing you into it (or even "presenting" them to you...you have your tools, you decide how to use them and deal with the potential consequences)

The game is full of secrets and jokes to be found here and there (take a look to the IRC logs), the story will keep you immersed from second 0 till the end of it.

Of course the game is not perfect, and I did personally miss some commands, like "cp" (copy files locally), "find" (self explanatory), and some way to create files and edit them beyond using "replace" on them.

I definitely recommend it: 9/10 

PS: Oh, you want some fast tips/hints? Get in fast, do/get what you need to, delete logs (always), get out.

$> post Review
$> cd /log

$> logout

review_text_raw:
First of all, I never played Uplink, so I can't compare this to that. What I did play was the HackRUN saga, so please pardon my comparison to a not very similar game. I also think it's funny that there are .dll and .exe file on what is (seemingly) a Linux system, but I can ignore that.

In a nutshell, Hacknet is a hacking sim game with a decent storyline. That is something I don't see often. HackRUN also has a storyline, but it's pretty linear if you ask me. This game uses real UNIX commands. For those of you new to the coding world (I guess?), it won't be hard to pick up; the tutorial does a good job of introducing the commands, and the 'help' menu will always be there to help you. For those of you who are familiar with the UNIX command prompt, you will be pleasantly surprised. The animations you get when hacking is pretty cool too. The best part of this games\ is that there are some systems that will start tracing you once you start your hacks. You have 100 seconds to do whatever you need to do and GTFO the system, or else (I don't actually know what happens because I have never failed doing so). You can, disconnect midway to cut the trace short and come back in the system again to do your stuff (again) at a later time, but hey, where's the fun in that? Along the way of making yourself a name in the hacking world (in the game), you will encounter files that are seemingly unimportant (like IRC log files, random text files, etc.). You are half right, [b]most[/b] of these files are unimportant. They may contain jokes and the stupidity of internet friends chatting together; but the rest may contain passwords that will make your life much easier when attempting to access some systems or useful information on your target's location.

There are decent puzzles in this game that happens in a specific scenario, but the contracts you get are pretty repetitive: [spoiler]probe the system, bypass proxy/firewall if those are there, open some ports, hack in, do your stuff, clear logs, get out[/spoiler]. New commands are introduced every now and then, but those have instructions along with them, so it's pretty easy to do whatever you need to do after. Basically, it's not very challenging (unless the devs add a "No x-server" mode to force you to use the command prompt throughout the game, that would be really fun, devs pls read). The last thing that this game lacks is the ability to adjust the SFX volume. Me clicking things actually shocks me sometimes because trust me, the SFXs are loud.

In conclusion, Hacknet is a good hacking sim with a decent storyline and a bit of realism. Would I recommend? Yes. Would I play again? Yes.

review_text_raw:
Got this game because it was on sale and I was interested in it being a hacking game. I was not disappointed and would pay full price for it hands down. By no means is this game super realistic, but it is definitely intriguing and fun. It uses some real Unix commands, and has a little sense of how hacking works in the real world, however it is still a game... but it felt like so much more than that. No prior hacking/computer science experience or knowledge is needed. The game teaches you from the get go with a tutorial on the basics of how to hack nodes in the game and a few of the commands you can use. All you have to do is type "help" if you forget a command. Also you can autofill commands with the tab key which really saves you some time.

The story is very captivating. There's quite a bit of plot to uncover all while you're exploring the network of loads of IPs. It's not exactly a sandbox but you do have a bit of freedom when it comes to certain missions or hacking methods. Every step of the way this game keeps you sucked in until you finally uncover every hole you can find. Once I got to the end, my mind was blown.

I currently have 16 hours in this game. I just started the Labyrinths DLC which is already proving to be worth the buy as well. You get different background music, more GUI themes, and brand new story and collection of nodes to explore. Once I finish the DLC I am definitely going back in for another playthrough. 

Overall I would give this game a 9/10. Some parts may seem a tad bit repetitive. But the game definitely makes up for it with a great dense story, killer music, and the awesome feeling of being immersed into a world where you can become an expert hacker

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a rare gem in the indie scene—a game that doesn't just simulate hacking, but immerses you in it with a level of authenticity and atmosphere that most genre attempts barely graze. Designed by Team Fractal Alligator, it's a terminal-based hacking simulator where you dive deep into a rabbit hole of digital espionage, underground networks, and cryptic puzzles, all communicated through a command-line interface. On paper, that may sound dry. In execution, it’s anything but.

What makes Hacknet such a standout experience, is its faithfulness to real-world logic without alienating player unfamiliar with coding. It teaches by doing, never hand-holding but never abandoning you either. You’ll boot systems, probe for vulnerabilities, crack passwords, and manipulate files—all with just a blinking cursor and your wits. There’s a certain thrill in executing a flawless sequence of commands under pressure, like defusing a bomb with only seconds to spare.

The most positive  consistently praise its atmosphere. The soundtrack—moody and immersive—drenches every hack in tension and mystery. The narrative, while not overly complex, feeds a constant sense of curiosity. You're not just following orders; you're unraveling a digital conspiracy. Describe the experience as “empowering,” especially for those who’ve never touched a line of code before. There’s a genuine sense of growth as you become more fluent in your digital arsenal.

That said, even the best-crafted code has bugs. Point out a few frustrating limitations. First, while the UI is stylistically perfect for the theme, it can become visually fatiguing over long sessions, especially when you're staring at lines of text with minimal interface variety. Second, once you grasp the core mechanics, the challenge can taper off. Some missions fall into predictable patterns, and may find the mid-to-late game lacking in complexity.

Additionally, the lack of real choice in how you approach objectives can feel constricting. While it feels like a sandbox at first glance, the game often funnels you into single-solution puzzles. Wishing for more freedom to experiment or “break the system” in creative ways.

Hacknet is a brilliant idea executed with style, but not without cracks in its shell. The story is intriguing, yet occasionally shallow; the pacing tight, though at times undermined by repetitiveness. Still, it’s universally acknowledged as an educational and atmospheric triumph, especially for those willing to sink into its digital depths.

Final Verdict:
Hacknet is a thinking person’s game—a methodical, immersive dive into the world of virtual infiltration. It empowers through minimalism, teaches through tension, and wraps it all in a darkly ambient package. Despite a few structural shortcomings, it stands tall as a uniquely engrossing experience.

Rating: 8.5/10
A captivating digital puzzle-box, slightly constrained by its own structure, but well worth unlocking.

review_text_raw:
The TL;DR on Hacknet is that this, (including or excluding it's DLC companion, Labyrinths, which is a sort of expansion pack) is a beautiful, self-contained little experience that an average gamer can knock out in a day or two whether or not that gamer has the DLC, which revolves around themes of death, privacy, freedom, security, and compromise, all within the conceit of a terminal-interface hacking simulator. 

I don't want to spoil all that much, frankly, but there's an amazing array of moments, missions, results of your actions, fantastic design, great music, delightful secrets, and more. The achievements list is short but meaningful instead of padded – one or two of the achievements here may double your playtime if you care to go for them, and you should. 

Some of you may be skeptical, having played other hacking sim type games and come away disappointed from them. You should be. This is a genre that, frankly, deserves much better in general than it has gotten from developers. Hacknet is, however, different. Hacknet is a game with a power story to tell that will take twists and turns that you do not expect, and resonates with each playthrough no less than it did the first time. 

Even if we were to disregard the story, Hacknet is mechanically incredible. It takes direct inspiration from the command lines of Linux-based operating systems – if you know what 'man' does, try typing it in-game, for just one non-spoiler example – and manages a fantastic level of immersion by removing layers of arbitration between the player and the game. There's no pressing 'w' or 'up' to run here – no running at all, in fact. 

This is one of those indie titles that basically every gamer should buy, play, beat, and complete, if at all possible. Don't miss out on this one.

You type commands(always the same few), wait a few seconds, skim through what you've gotta skim, turn the current assignment in, rinse and repeat.

Sadly, the game lacks any real player agency: You're just following a series of steps with minimal variation, with no real difficulty to speak of at any point, and no freedom, be it to approach things differently, or do something for your own reasons.

I'm frankly baffled at how so many people recommend it, it's essentially a nongame.
